newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China wheat buying possible, but limited - trade.
newsitem.headline: China wheat buying possible, but limited - trade.

text.p: Asian grain traders said on Tuesday it was unlikely China had bought up to 1.5 million tonnes of Canadian wheat as rumoured in the North American market, but added there were shortages of high quality wheat.
"I haven't heard anything of that sort, I don't think China would buy so much" said one grain trader, echoing the views of many others.

Talk circulated in the Canadian and Chicago grain markets over the weekend that China had bought between 500,000 to 1.5 million tonnes of Canadian wheat for June/July shipment and about 23,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat.
The Canadian Wheat Board declined to comment on the rumours.
One U.S. exporter termed the reports "old news", saying the Chinese had rolled over some of their old-crop Canadian purchases into new crop.
Traders said in February China may have bought about 500,000 tonnes of Canadian wheat in December, for delivery in March, April and May.
China's wheat crop year runs from July 1 to June 30, while the European and U.S. crop years run from June 1 to May 30.
"With the transit time for grain going from the U.S., or Europe, to China, our crop year and their crop year fit almost exactly," one trader said.
According to one China-based source, a cargo of between 10,000 to 15,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat was heard sold last week to a joint venture in China, probably for prompt delivery in April or May.
China's wheat import quota is split into separate categories for joint ventures and for state importers on behalf of the Grain Bureau, he said .
"I think the joint ventures have some quota," the trader said, adding his estimate for wheat quota currently available under this category was around 200,000 tonnes.

Some sources said they would not be surprised if China had bought some wheat, given that there had been hardly any imports in the past few months, but most said China's wheat supplies were ample following a bumper harvest and there had been no talk of new wheat import quotas being issued.
"The Chinese government would prefer to use domestic wheat," one senior grains trader said.
Other traders in Hong Kong and China said end users, particularly in the southern province of Guangdong, had complained about a shortage of high quality wheat.
Traders generally estimated China would import about five million tonnes of wheat in the 1997/98 crop year, although one source pegged the level at below four million tonnes.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture projected China's 1997/98 wheat imports at six million tonnes.
According to customs figures, China imported about 270,000 tonnes of wheat in January and February, down 74.6 percent from the same period last year.
